summary: Revenue management, service automation, and demand forecasting lead adoption - and AI assistants are becoming a discovery channel hotels now compete inside of. Who tracks it: the sector's research firms, its standards and trade bodies, and the platforms actually running pricing and guest operations.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use among accommodation and food-services firms at 8.6 percent in its latest reading, up from 8.3 percent in the prior period, making it one of the relatively lower-adoption sectors the survey covers. That figure comes directly from firms answering whether they used AI in the preceding two weeks, so it reflects active, operational deployment rather than stated intent, and it suggests that while the direction of travel is upward, most hospitality businesses have not yet integrated AI into day-to-day workflows.

Where adoption is happening, it tends to concentrate in guest-facing and operations-facing layers simultaneously. Canary, whose hospitality management software is trusted by more than 20,000 hotels worldwide per its own reporting, ships AI across guest messaging, check-in, and revenue-adjacent functions, integrating natively with major property management systems. Skift Research, which tracks digital maturity across hotels, airlines, online travel agencies, and short-term rentals, characterizes agentic AI as capable of upending the travel industry, and has published analysis on what it calls AI-compressed discovery funnels, the idea that hotel brands now compete not just on price and location but on whether AI assistants surface them at all.

That last point has become a measurable competitive dimension on its own. HotelWorld AI's quarterly World's Best at AI Index, covering more than 2,105 hotel brands and 131,000 properties globally, tracks how often hotel brands appear in AI-generated recommendations across ChatGPT, Google AI Overview, Perplexity, and Claude. Its Q1 2026 update finds that only a small minority of hotels appear in AI-generated shortlists at all, and describes AI visibility as the industry's next competitive battleground. HotelWorld AI frames the shift plainly: travelers no longer scroll through search results but ask AI assistants and receive a shortlist, meaning distribution strategy now has an answer-engine optimization layer alongside traditional search engine optimization.

On the food-service side, the National Restaurant Association tracks AI and automation across restaurant and quick-service chains, covering areas such as AI-driven drive-thru ordering, kitchen robotics, and predictive ordering, though its publicly accessible pages skew toward advocacy and culinary trend forecasting rather than publishing specific adoption percentages. The American Hotel and Lodging Association, which absorbed the HTNG technology standards body and now houses hotel-systems interoperability work, focuses its public-facing activity on workforce development, sustainability, and federal advocacy rather than releasing AI-specific deployment data, so the linkage between standards work and measurable AI rollout remains indirect from publicly available sources.

For an operator weighing whether to deploy, the Census figure suggests the industry is still early enough that first movers retain a genuine differentiation window, particularly in AI-driven guest discovery. Skift Research notes that the next phase of hotel competition will reward brands that drive pricing power, loyalty relevance, and visibility in AI-compressed discovery funnels, which implies the risk of inaction compounds over time as AI assistants harden their recommendation patterns. At the same time, the low headline adoption rate and the absence of published ROI benchmarks from the sector's main trade bodies mean that operators should expect to build their own business cases rather than rely on industry-wide proof points.
